content:
The Trump administration has quietly shelved proposals to use business deals as an incentive for Russia to end its war in Ukraine, after the Kremlin showed little interest in the proposed ventures, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday.

According to the newspaper, which cited five officials briefed on the change in tactic, President Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have told European officials that corporate tie-ups are no longer a core aspect of the US pitch to Moscow. The focus, the officials said, has shifted to territory and security.

In recent months, Witkoff and Kushner had floated a series of post-war commercial ventures designed to give Russian President Vladimir Putin a financial reason to stop the fighting. The ideas included US investment in Russian oil projects and titanium production, alongside a resumption of pipeline gas supplies to Europe, according to the Financial Times. Energy and aviation were the two sectors at the centre of the pitch.

The reporting, carried by [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/us-shelves-proposals-use-business-deals-with-russia-end-ukraine-war-ft-reports-2026-11-25/), adds an important detail that most of the early coverage has glossed over: Russian officials initially embraced the proposals. The sources said Moscow saw the prospect of business deals as a way to hold Trump's attention while the diplomacy played out. That enthusiasm has since faded, even as the Kremlin has kept its demands for Ukrainian territory and other concessions that Kyiv regards as unacceptable.

The turning point appears to have come at the latest round of talks in Abu Dhabi earlier in November. There, according to the officials, Russian negotiators showed little appetite for the commercial offers and reinforced their hardline position, telling the Americans that such arrangements would not persuade Putin to soften his demands.

"It was made pretty clear that [the Russians] were not in the market for this kind of thing," one of the officials told the newspaper.

Other US officials have concluded that Putin is not driven by business interests in his pursuit of victory in the war. "The Americans have gradually come to get a better understanding of what the sides of the conflict need," another source said, in a remark that captures how far Washington's reading of Moscow has moved since the commercial pitch was first drawn up.

The strategy of economic deals was, in the words of one official, put "on the back burner", and the United States has shifted to what the sources described as a "more traditional" approach to negotiation, focused on the "land for peace" principle. A source familiar with Putin's thinking said the Kremlin leader has no intention of agreeing to any deal that does not include further territorial concessions from Ukraine.

That framing sets up the central dilemma of the talks. The same source sketched what a deal might look like from Moscow's perspective: "If what they are offering is de facto Article 5 without NATO, and Zelenskyy gives up Donbas, this is actually really quite a good deal for Ukraine. Any security guarantees for Ukraine involve giving up territory at some point and the Ukrainians do understand this."

The shift matters because the business-deal pitch was never a minor side idea. It was the mechanism by which the administration hoped to make a settlement attractive to Putin without forcing Kyiv into concessions it could not accept. Its failure leaves the negotiation where it has always been stuck: on the question of how much land Ukraine would have to surrender, and what security guarantees would be worth having in return. Russia has revived sweeping demands on European security in parallel with the talks, as Global Wire [reported earlier this month](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/russia-revives-2021-nato-demands-european-security-november-2026), underscoring how far apart the two sides remain on the fundamentals.

The Financial Times had previously reported that the Trump administration told European and Ukrainian officials it wants Ukraine and Russia to reach a peace agreement by the beginning of January 2027. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview with Bloomberg that Kushner and Witkoff are pushing for a deal as soon as possible, ideally by January, remarks that Trump publicly laughed off.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report, and Reuters said it could not immediately verify it. The Kremlin has not commented publicly on the shelved proposals.

The development comes as the war itself grinds on. Putin said on Tuesday that Ukraine continues to attack Russian oil refineries despite requests from Trump to hold off, and pledged retaliation. European governments, meanwhile, continue to fund Kyiv directly: the EU disbursed a record sum to Ukraine earlier this month, as Global Wire [reported](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/eu-disburses-record-7-9-billion-ukraine-november-2026), a reminder that the financial and military backing for Ukraine does not depend on the fate of the American peace initiative.

For now, the message from the Abu Dhabi talks is stark. Moscow is not, as one official put it, in the market for business deals. The negotiation has returned to its hardest ground: territory, and the security guarantees that would have to follow any settlement.
summary: The Trump administration has quietly dropped proposals to lure Russia into ending the war in Ukraine with lucrative energy and aviation deals, after the Kremlin showed little interest, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday. Washington's focus has now shifted to the far harder questions of territory and security guarantees.
title: US shelves business deals as bait for Russia as Ukraine peace push turns to territory and security
